mainTopic: End of the teaching about the 974 'snatched' generations, a second reading of אשר קומטו as praise for תלמידי חכמים, two views on how מלאכים are created, and resolving the white-hair vs. black-hair פסוקים describing הקדוש ברוך הוא.
overview: This amud opens by finishing a teaching about 974 generations that were never created; הקדוש ברוך הוא planted some of them in every generation as the עזי פנים. רב נחמן בר יצחק then reads the same פסוק as praise for תלמידי חכמים who wear themselves out for תורה and are shown secrets in עולם הבא. Next come two views on how מלאכים are created: daily from נהר דינור (רב) or from every word ה׳ speaks (רבי יונתן). The גמרא resolves clashing פסוקים about white and black hair (in the ישיבה versus at war), and about one throne versus thrones, where רבי עקיבא, רבי יוסי הגלילי and רבי אלעזר בן עזריה each explain the second throne differently. Then רב דימי teaches ישעיה's eighteen curses, and the גמרא explains each item in ישעיהו 3 as a type of Torah scholar or leader whose loss is a curse, ending with empty, careless people mocking those full of מצוות. רב קטינא learns from ישעיהו 3:6-7 that trustworthy people remained even at ירושלים's fall, and the גמרא defends his proof. Finally, רבא seems to say the opposite, and the גמרא begins to answer with 'לא קשיא'; the answer continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The unborn generations are planted among us as the brazen ones
steps.stepSummary: Finishing an earlier teaching: the generations that were meant to exist but never did were spread by הקדוש ברוך הוא into every generation, and they are the עזי פנים.
steps.simpleTranslation: …before the world was created, but they were never created. So הקדוש ברוך הוא planted some of them in every single generation, and they are the brazen people of each generation.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a teaching that started just before this section, about 974 generations that were 'snatched away' before they were ever created. It adds that some of those souls were placed in every generation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first teaching read the word קומטו as 'snatched away': those generations lost their chance to exist. This line adds a result: they did not vanish completely. They show up scattered through history as the עזי פנים, people with a brazen, chutzpadik nature.
steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new teaching. It is the end of a statement that began before this section, so 'they' means the 974 generations that were never created.

phrases.english: before the world was created, but they were not created.
phrases.notes: 'They' are the 974 generations from the teaching just before this, which were meant to be created but were cut off.

phrases.english: The Holy One, Blessed be He, arose and planted them
in each and every generation,
and they are the brazen ones of the generation.

steps.triggerLanguage: עָמַד הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא וּשְׁתָלָן בְּכׇל דּוֹר וָדוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the earlier explanation of אשר קומטו ולא עת, which began before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The souls of the uncreated generations were scattered into every generation and show up as the עזי פנים.

steps.title: A positive reading: Torah scholars who wear themselves out
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק reads אשר קומטו as praise for תלמידי חכמים who shrink themselves for תורה, and they are rewarded with secrets in עולם הבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said: the פסוק 'who were shriveled' is written as a blessing. It refers to תלמידי חכמים who wear themselves down over תורה in this world. הקדוש ברוך הוא will reveal secrets to them in עולם הבא, as it says: 'A river poured out their foundation (יסודם).'
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן בר יצחק gives a completely different reading of the same פסוק. He reads it as a compliment, not a curse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first approach read קומטו as 'snatched away,' something bad. רב נחמן בר יצחק reads it as 'shriveled': scholars who give up comfort and wear themselves out for learning. He then reads יסודם in the second half of the פסוק as a hint to סוד, a secret, which is their reward.

keyTerms.meaning: A secret (hinted in the word יְסוֹדָם)

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows how one פסוק can carry two opposite readings, one about people who lost out and one about people who sacrificed for תורה.

phrases.english: And Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said:
'Who were shriveled' is written as a blessing.
These are Torah scholars

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁמְּקַמְּטִין עַצְמָן עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה,
phrases.english: who shrivel themselves over the words of Torah in this world;

phrases.aramaic: הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מְגַלֶּה לָהֶם סוֹד
phrases.english: The Holy One, Blessed be He, reveals a secret to them
in the World to Come, as it says: 'A river poured out their foundation.'
phrases.notes: Same פסוק. He hears the word סוד, 'secret,' inside יסודם.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers an opposite, positive reading of the same פסוק explained in step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אשר קומטו refers to תלמידי חכמים who sacrifice for תורה and will be shown secrets in עולם הבא.

steps.title: New angels are created every day from the River of Fire
steps.stepSummary: שמואל tells חייא בר רב a teaching of his father רב: every day מלאכי השרת are created from נהר דינור, sing שירה, and then cease to exist.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said to חייא בר רב: 'Son of a lion! Come, let me tell you one of the fine teachings your father used to say. Every day מלאכי השרת are created from the River of Fire. They sing to ה׳ and then disappear, as it says: "They are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness."'
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל shares a teaching of רב with רב's son. New angels are made each day, sing once, and are gone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The source is the פסוק 'new every morning.' רב reads 'new' as new angels created each day to praise ה׳. These angels exist only to sing their one song, and then they end.

keyTerms.meaning: Son of a lion, a title of honor for the son of a great man

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ שְׁמוּאֵל לְחִיָּיא בַּר רַב:
phrases.english: Shmuel said to Chiyya bar Rav:
Son of a lion!
phrases.notes: A warm compliment, roughly 'son of a great man.'

phrases.english: Come, let me tell you a thing

phrases.aramaic: מֵהָנֵי מִילֵּי מְעַלְּיָיתָא דַּהֲוָה אָמַר אֲבוּךְ:
phrases.english: from those fine teachings that your father used to say:

phrases.aramaic: כֹּל יוֹמָא וְיוֹמָא נִבְרָאִין מַלְאֲכֵי הַשָּׁרֵת
phrases.english: Each and every day ministering angels are created
from the River of Fire,
and they say song and then cease to exist,
as it says: 'They are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ שְׁמוּאֵל לְחִיָּיא בַּר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: how angels are created.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Each day new מלאכי השרת are created from נהר דינור, sing, and cease to exist.

steps.title: A disagreement: angels come from ה׳'s words
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that רב's view disagrees with רבי שמואל בר נחמני in the name of רבי יונתן, who says a מלאך is created from every word ה׳ speaks.
steps.simpleTranslation: This disagrees with רבי שמואל בר נחמני. He said in the name of רבי יונתן: from every single word that comes out of the mouth of הקדוש ברוך הוא, one angel is created, as it says: 'By the word of ה׳ the heavens were made, and by the breath of His mouth all their hosts.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that a different אמורא holds another view of where angels come from. It brings his statement and his פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב said angels come from נהר דינור. רבי יונתן says they come from ה׳'s speech, reading 'all their hosts' as the angels made by 'the breath of His mouth.' The גמרא only notes the disagreement and does not decide between them.
steps.whatToRemember: There are two views on how angels are created: daily from נהר דינור (רב), or from each word of ה׳‎ (רבי יונתן).

phrases.english: And this disagrees with Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani.

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן:
phrases.english: For Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said in the name of Rabbi Yonatan:
Each and every word
that comes out of the mouth of the Holy One, Blessed be He,
one angel is created from it,
as it says: 'By the word of ה׳ the heavens were made,
and by the breath of His mouth all their hosts.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that step 3's view is disputed and brings the opposing view.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי יונתן, an angel is created from every word ה׳ speaks.

steps.title: Two verses clash: white hair or black hair?
steps.stepSummary: One פסוק in דניאל describes ה׳ with hair white as wool, while a פסוק in שיר השירים describes black, curly locks.
steps.simpleTranslation: One פסוק says: 'His clothing was white as snow, and the hair of His head like clean wool.' Another פסוק says: 'His locks are curly, black as a raven'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets two פסוקים side by side that seem to contradict each other. The answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both פסוקים are images of how ה׳ appears. White hair suggests an old man and black hair suggests a young man. Both images cannot seem true at the same time.

keyTerms.meaning: One פסוק says (opening of a contradiction between פסוקים)

phrases.english: One verse says:
'His clothing was white as snow,
and the hair of His head like clean wool.'
And it is written: 'His locks are curly,
black as a raven'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: a contradiction between two פסוקים.
steps.kashyaTarget: The two descriptions of ה׳'s hair in דניאל and שיר השירים.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: White hair (old) and black hair (young) seem to describe the same subject in opposite ways.

steps.title: In the yeshiva versus at war
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the white-hair image describes ה׳ in the ישיבה, and the black-hair image describes Him at war.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not a problem. One פסוק describes Him in the ישיבה, and the other describes Him at war.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the contradiction by assigning each פסוק to a different situation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two images are not about the same moment. In the ישיבה ה׳ is pictured as a wise elder with white hair. In battle He is pictured as a strong young man with black hair.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult; there is no contradiction
Here... here (each source refers to a different case)
The heavenly academy, a place of learning

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
Here it is in the yeshiva; here it is at war.
phrases.notes: White hair (דניאל) is the ישיבה. Black hair (שיר השירים) is war.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא: כָּאן בִּישִׁיבָה, כָּאן בַּמִּלְחָמָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases: each פסוק describes a different setting.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both פסוקים describe ה׳ in the same way, so they contradict each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: The white-hair image fits the ישיבה and the black-hair image fits war.

steps.title: Why old fits the yeshiva and young fits war
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא supports its answer with a saying: nothing is finer in the ישיבה than an elder, and nothing is finer in war than a young man.
steps.simpleTranslation: As the Master said: nothing is finer in the ישיבה than an old man, and nothing is finer in war than a young man.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up the answer from step 6 with a known saying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The saying explains why each image matches its setting. Age brings wisdom, which suits learning. Youth brings strength, which suits battle.
steps.whatToRemember: The white-hair and black-hair images do not contradict each other. One shows ה׳ as the wise elder in the ישיבה, the other as the young warrior at war.

phrases.english: As the Master said:

phrases.aramaic: אֵין לְךָ נָאֶה בִּישִׁיבָה אֶלָּא זָקֵן,
phrases.english: there is nothing finer in the yeshiva than an old man,

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵין לְךָ נָאֶה בַּמִּלְחָמָה אֶלָּא בָּחוּר.
phrases.english: and there is nothing finer in war than a young man.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer given in step 6.
steps.raayaObject: The answer that white hair fits the ישיבה and black hair fits war.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A known saying (דאמר מר) that an elder suits the ישיבה and a young man suits war.

steps.title: One throne or many thrones?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that one phrase in דניאל speaks of ה׳'s single throne, while another phrase speaks of thrones in the plural.
steps.simpleTranslation: One verse says: 'His throne was fiery flames,' and another verse says: 'Until thrones were placed, and the Ancient of Days sat!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new contradiction between two phrases about ה׳'s throne. One phrase says one throne, the other says thrones.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This works just like the hair contradiction in Step 5. If ה׳ sits on one throne, why does the פסוק say 'thrones' in the plural? The question is: who or what is the second throne for?

keyTerms.meaning: the Ancient of Days, a name for ה׳ in דניאל

phrases.english: One verse says:
"His throne was fiery flames,"
and one verse says:
"Until thrones were placed,"
phrases.notes: This is the same פסוק. The word 'thrones' is plural, and that is the whole problem.

phrases.english: "and the Ancient of Days sat!"

steps.triggerLanguage: כָּתוּב אֶחָד אוֹמֵר וְכָתוּב אֶחָד אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new contradiction in the same vision of דניאל, built the same way as Step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: The plain reading of the פסוק in דניאל
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A single throne and plural thrones in the same vision seem to clash.

steps.title: One throne for ה׳, one for דוד
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that there are two thrones: one for ה׳ and one for דוד.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult: one throne is for Him, and one is for דוד.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the contradiction. ה׳'s own throne is the single one, and the second throne belongs to דוד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With this answer both phrases are true. 'His throne' means ה׳'s own seat, and 'thrones' counts the second seat too.

keyTerms.meaning: it is not difficult (the question has an answer)

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
one is for Him and one is for David.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction in Step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Two different subjects: each word refers to a different throne
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק speaks of only one throne, so the plural makes no sense.
steps.terutzMaskana: There are two thrones, one for ה׳ and one for דוד.

steps.title: A ברייתא: this is רבי עקיבא's view
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא shows that its answer comes from a ברייתא, where רבי עקיבא says it.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is taught in a ברייתא: 'One for Him and one for דוד.' These are the words of רבי עקיבא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up its answer by quoting a ברייתא. This also sets up the next step, where another תנא argues.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer in Step 9 was not made up by the גמרא. It is the view of רבי עקיבא. Naming him matters because the next lines show how other תנאים react to his idea.

keyTerms.meaning: as it was taught in a ברייתא

phrases.english: As it is taught:
One is for Him and one is for David;
these are the words of Rabbi Akiva.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer of Step 9 with a ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: The answer 'one for Him and one for דוד'

steps.title: רבי יוסי הגלילי objects: judgment and kindness
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי הגלילי rejects the idea of a throne for דוד and says the two thrones are one for judgment and one for kindness.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי הגלילי said to him: עקיבא, how long will you treat the שכינה as ordinary? Rather, one throne is for judgment and one is for kindness.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי הגלילי strongly disagrees with רבי עקיבא and gives a different explanation of the two thrones.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His problem is that seating a person next to ה׳ makes the שכינה seem ordinary. So he keeps both thrones but says they are both ה׳'s, used in two ways: one for דין and one for צדקה.
steps.confusionAlert: Both thrones are now ה׳'s. The second throne is not for another person anymore. It shows a different way that ה׳ acts.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili said to him:
Akiva, how long
will you make the Divine Presence ordinary?!
Rather: one is for judgment and one is for kindness.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ רַבִּי יוֹסֵי הַגְּלִילִי עֲקִיבָא עַד מָתַי אַתָּה עוֹשֶׂה שְׁכִינָה חוֹל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רבי עקיבא's explanation from Step 10 and offers a new one.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The idea that the second throne is for דוד
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It lessens the honor of the שכינה by seating a person next to ה׳.

steps.title: Did רבי עקיבא accept this?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether רבי עקיבא agreed with רבי יוסי הגלילי's correction.
steps.simpleTranslation: Did he accept it from him, or did he not accept it from him?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a simple question about what happened next: did רבי עקיבא change his mind? This sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא only tells us that רבי יוסי הגלילי objected. The גמרא wants to know if רבי עקיבא then took on the new explanation.

phrases.aramaic: קַיבְּלַהּ מִינֵּיהּ, אוֹ לָא קַיבְּלַהּ מִינֵּיהּ?
phrases.english: Did he accept it from him, or did he not accept it from him?

steps.triggerLanguage: קַיבְּלַהּ מִינֵּיהּ אוֹ לָא קַיבְּלַהּ מִינֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the result of the disagreement in Step 11.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether רבי עקיבא gave up his view and accepted 'judgment and kindness.'

steps.title: Yes: another ברייתא quotes רבי עקיבא saying judgment and kindness
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא where רבי עקיבא himself says 'one for judgment and one for kindness,' which shows he accepted it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: 'One for judgment and one for kindness.' These are the words of רבי עקיבא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question with another ברייתא. There, רבי עקיבא teaches רבי יוסי הגלילי's explanation as his own.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since רבי עקיבא now says 'judgment and kindness,' he must have accepted the correction. This ברייתא continues, and the next step shows another תנא disagreeing.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
One is for judgment and one is for kindness;
these are the words of Rabbi Akiva.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 12.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי עקיבא accepted it, since another ברייתא has him saying 'judgment and kindness.'

steps.title: רבי אלעזר בן עזריה: a seat and a footstool
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר בן עזריה tells רבי עקיבא to stick to his strong areas and explains the two thrones as a seat and a footstool, based on a פסוק in ישעיהו.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר בן עזריה said to him: עקיבא, what are you doing with אגדה? Take your words to נגעים and אהלות. Rather, one is a seat and one is a footstool. The seat is to sit on, and the footstool is for His feet, as it says: 'The heavens are My seat and the earth is My footstool.'
steps.whatsHappening: Another תנא rejects even the 'judgment and kindness' explanation. He says one 'throne' is a seat and the other is a footstool.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר בן עזריה tells רבי עקיבא that his real strength is in hard הלכות like נגעים and אהלות, not אגדה. His own answer is that the plural 'thrones' means a seat plus a footstool. He proves this from ישעיהו, which speaks of ה׳'s seat and footstool together.

keyTerms.meaning: אגדה, the non-legal teachings of Torah
hard topics of טומאה: צרעת and טומאת מת

steps.whatToRemember: Three views of the two thrones: (1) ה׳ and דוד, (2) judgment and kindness, (3) a seat and a footstool.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לוֹ רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן עֲזַרְיָה:
phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya said to him:
Akiva, what are you doing with aggada!
Take your words
to plagues and tents.
phrases.notes: These are hard areas of טומאה: צרעת, and טומאת מת under one roof. He means 'that is your real strength.'

phrases.english: Rather: one is a seat and one is a footstool.
The seat is to sit on,
the footstool is to rest His feet,
as it says: "The heavens are My seat,"
"and the earth is My footstool."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן עֲזַרְיָה עֲקִיבָא מָה לְךָ אֵצֶל הַגָּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the 'judgment and kindness' answer from Step 13 and gives a final explanation.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The explanation 'one for judgment and one for kindness'
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: He says אגדה is not רבי עקיבא's field, and he gives a simpler reading backed by a פסוק.

steps.title: רב דימי: ישעיה's eighteen curses
steps.stepSummary: רב דימי teaches that ישעיה cursed ישראל with eighteen curses and was not satisfied until he said: 'The young will be bold against the old.'
steps.simpleTranslation: When רב דימי came, he said: ישעיה cursed ישראל with eighteen curses, and his mind did not calm down until he told them this verse: 'The young will be bold against the old, and the lowly against the honored.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new teaching. רב דימי says ישעיה gave eighteen curses, and the worst one, which finally satisfied him, was young people disrespecting elders.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This shows how serious it is when the young and lowly act boldly toward the old and honored. ישעיה saw it as worse than all eighteen curses before it. The גמרא now turns to the פסוקים in ישעיהו 3, the same chapter it quoted earlier for 'שר חמשים' and 'נשוא פנים'.

keyTerms.meaning: when he came (from ארץ ישראל to בבל)
his mind calmed down, he was satisfied
they will act boldly, with chutzpah

phrases.english: When Rav Dimi came, he said:
Eighteen curses
Isaiah cursed Israel with,
and his mind did not calm down
until he told them this verse:
"The young will be bold against the old,"
"and the lowly against the honored."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the thrones discussion ends, the גמרא turns to ישעיהו 3, the passage behind the earlier requirement of 'שר חמשים ונשוא פנים.'
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ישעיה's eighteen curses were capped by the worst one: the young and lowly acting boldly toward the old and honored.

steps.title: What are the eighteen curses?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which eighteen curses רב דימי means.
steps.simpleTranslation: The eighteen curses, what are they?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the list of curses that רב דימי mentioned. This sets up the next step, where the פסוקים are quoted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב דימי gave a number but no list. The גמרא wants to know where in ישעיהו these eighteen curses are found.

phrases.english: The eighteen curses, what are they?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the details of רב דימי's statement.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source and list of the eighteen curses.

steps.title: The list in ישעיהו: everything taken away
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the פסוקים in ישעיהו that list everything ה׳ will take away from ירושלים and יהודה, ending with children ruling over them.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: 'For behold, the Master, ה׳ of hosts, will take away from ירושלים and from יהודה support and staff, every support of bread and every support of water; the mighty man and the man of war, the judge, the prophet, the diviner and the elder; the captain of fifty, the man of favor, the counselor, the skilled craftsman and the one wise in whispering. And I will make youths their princes, and babes will rule over them,' and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by quoting the פסוקים. Each thing listed that ה׳ will take away counts as one of the curses.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The list moves from food and water, to soldiers, to judges and wise people, and ends with children ruling the people. That ending leads straight into the פסוק רב דימי quoted, about the young being bold against the old.

keyTerms.meaning: support and staff (things people lean on)
one wise in whispering, who understands hidden things

steps.whyThisMatters: This list includes 'שר חמשים' and 'נשוא פנים,' terms the גמרא uses for the kind of person allowed to learn the secrets of Torah. That makes the list important for the larger sugya.
steps.whatToRemember: The eighteen curses are things ה׳ takes away from ישראל, and the climax is the young and lowly having no respect for the old and honored.

phrases.english: As it is written: "For behold, the Master, the Lord of hosts,"
"takes away from Jerusalem and from Judah"
"support and staff,"
"every support of bread"
"and every support of water;"
"the mighty man and the man of war,"
"the judge, the prophet, the diviner, and the elder;"
"the captain of fifty and the man of favor,"
"the counselor, the skilled craftsman, and the one wise in whispering."
"And I will make youths their princes,"
"and babes shall rule over them, etc."

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּכְתִיב כִּי הִנֵּה הָאָדוֹן ה׳ צְבָאוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 16 by quoting the פסוקים.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The curses are the items listed in ישעיהו 3:1–4 that ה׳ will take away from ישראל.

steps.title: Support and staff mean masters of Scripture and of משנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins explaining the פסוק: 'משען' refers to masters of מקרא, and 'משענה' refers to masters of משנה, like רבי יהודה בן תימא and his colleagues.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Support' means people who are experts in Scripture. 'Staff' means people who are experts in משנה, such as רבי יהודה בן תימא and his friends.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts going word by word through the פסוק it just quoted. It explains the first two words as two kinds of Torah experts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says ה׳ will remove 'משען ומשענה', the support and the staff. The גמרא reads these as the people who hold up the nation spiritually. The masculine form is experts in מקרא, and the feminine form is experts in משנה.

phrases.english: 'Support': these are the masters of Scripture.
phrases.notes: This is the first word in ישעיהו 3:1, the פסוק the גמרא just quoted.

phrases.english: 'Staff': these are the masters of Mishnah,

phrases.aramaic: כְּגוֹן רַבִּי יְהוּדָה בֶּן תֵּימָא וַחֲבֵירָיו.
phrases.english: such as Rabbi Yehudah ben Teima and his colleagues.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins explaining the פסוקים quoted in step 17.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: משען means masters of מקרא; משענה means masters of משנה.

steps.title: How many orders of משנה they knew
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא and the רבנן disagree about how many orders of משנה רבי יהודה בן תימא and his colleagues knew: six hundred or seven hundred.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא and the רבנן argue. One says they knew six hundred orders of משנה, and the other says seven hundred.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pauses for a side point about רבי יהודה בן תימא and his colleagues. It tells us how huge their knowledge of משנה was.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We have only six orders of משנה today. This dispute shows that these earlier masters knew far more, hundreds of orders. That helps explain why losing such people is a real curse.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa and the Rabbis disagree about this:

phrases.aramaic: חַד אָמַר: שֵׁשׁ מֵאוֹת סִדְרֵי מִשְׁנָה,
phrases.english: one said: six hundred orders of Mishnah,

phrases.aramaic: וְחַד אָמַר: שְׁבַע מֵאוֹת סִדְרֵי מִשְׁנָה.
phrases.english: and the other said: seven hundred orders of Mishnah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A side remark about the masters of משנה mentioned in step 18.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: These masters knew either 600 or 700 orders of משנה.

steps.title: Bread means masters of Talmud, water means masters of Aggadah
steps.stepSummary: 'Every support of bread' means masters of תלמוד, based on a פסוק in משלי. 'Every support of water' means masters of אגדה, who draw people's hearts like water.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Every support of bread' means experts in תלמוד, as it says, 'Come, eat of my bread and drink of the wine I mixed.' 'Every support of water' means experts in אגדה, who draw a person's heart like water.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to explaining the פסוק. It reads 'bread' and 'water' as two more kinds of Torah experts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Bread stands for תלמוד because a פסוק in משלי calls Torah 'my bread.' Water stands for אגדה because אגדה pulls a person's heart along the way water flows.

keyTerms.meaning: Masters of תלמוד (the analysis of the משנה)
Masters of אגדה (Torah stories and teachings that aren't הלכה)

phrases.english: 'Every support of bread': these are the masters of Talmud,
as it is stated: 'Come, eat of my bread,'
'and drink of the wine that I have mixed.'
'And every support of water': these are the masters of Aggadah,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁמּוֹשְׁכִין לִבּוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם כַּמַּיִם בְּאַגָּדָה.
phrases.english: who draw a person's heart like water with Aggadah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns from the side remark to continue explaining the פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Bread means masters of תלמוד; water means masters of אגדה.

steps.title: Mighty man, man of war, judge, prophet, diviner and elder
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains six more terms: the mighty man knows traditions, the man of war debates Torah, the judge judges truly, the prophet is plain, the diviner is a king, and the elder is fit to head a ישיבה.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Mighty man' is one who knows many received teachings. 'Man of war' is one who knows how to argue in the battle of Torah. 'Judge' is a judge who judges with complete truth. 'Prophet' means just what it says. 'Diviner' is a king, as it says, 'A divine word is on the lips of a king.' 'Elder' is someone fit to head a ישיבה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues through the list in ישעיהו 3:2, giving a quick meaning for each word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Most of these words sound like soldiers or officials, but the גמרא reads them as Torah roles. 'Prophet' is the one word taken at face value. 'Diviner' is a king because a פסוק in משלי connects קסם with a king's words.

keyTerms.meaning: To discuss and debate (literally 'to take and give')
A judgment that is completely true

phrases.english: 'Mighty man': this is a master of received traditions.
'And man of war': this is one who knows how to discuss and debate
in the battle of Torah.

phrases.aramaic: ״שׁוֹפֵט״ — זֶה דַּיָּין שֶׁדָּן דִּין אֱמֶת לַאֲמִיתּוֹ.
phrases.english: 'Judge': this is a judge who judges a true judgment truthfully.
'Prophet': as it literally means.
'Diviner': this is a king,
as it is stated: 'A divine sentence is on the lips of the king.'
'Elder': this is one fit to head an academy.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the word-by-word explanation of the פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Each title in the פסוק describes a type of Torah scholar or leader; only 'prophet' is meant literally.

steps.title: Captain of fifty read as master of the five books
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rereads 'שר חמשים' as 'שר חומשין': someone who can discuss all five books of the תורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Captain of fifty': don't read it as 'captain of fifty,' but as 'captain of the חומשים.' This is someone who knows how to discuss all five books of the תורה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא uses an אל תקרי, a reading trick that changes the vowels, to turn 'fifty' into 'the five books.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: חמשים (fifty) and חומשין (fifths, the five books) share the same letters. Changing the vowels changes a military rank into a Torah scholar who has mastered every חומש.

keyTerms.meaning: Don't read it as… (a reading with changed vowels)
The five books of the תורה

steps.confusionAlert: אל תקרי does not change the actual words of the פסוק. It adds an extra layer of meaning on top of the plain reading.

phrases.english: 'Captain of fifty': do not read it as 'sar chamishim,'
rather as 'sar chumashin.'
phrases.notes: Same letters, different vowels: 'fifty' becomes 'the חומשים.'

phrases.english: This is one who knows how to discuss and debate
in the five books of the Torah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues to the next term in the פסוק (ישעיהו 3:3).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שר חמשים means someone who has mastered the five חומשים.

steps.title: A second reading: a public speaker must be fifty
steps.stepSummary: Another explanation of 'captain of fifty' follows רבי אבהו, who learns from here that a מתורגמן for the public must be at least fifty years old.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another explanation: 'captain of fifty' follows רבי אבהו. רבי אבהו said: from here we learn that we don't appoint a מתורגמן over the public if he is under fifty.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a second way to read 'captain of fifty.' This time 'fifty' stays fifty, but it refers to age.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first reading 'fifty' became 'the five books.' Here the number is kept, and רבי אבהו learns a practical rule from it: the person who announces the Torah teaching to the public must be at least fifty years old.

keyTerms.meaning: The person who repeats and explains the teacher's words aloud to the crowd

steps.whyThisMatters: This turns a word in a curse into a real rule about who may serve the public.

phrases.english: Another explanation: 'captain of fifty' follows Rabbi Abbahu.
For Rabbi Abbahu said:

phrases.aramaic: מִכָּאן שֶׁאֵין מַעֲמִידִין מְתוּרְגְּמָן עַל הַצִּבּוּר
phrases.english: From here we learn that one does not appoint a disseminator over the public
if he is less than fifty years old.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second, different reading of the same term from step 22.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A מתורגמן for the public must be at least fifty years old.

steps.title: The man of favor: a person whose merit protects his generation
steps.stepSummary: 'נשוא פנים' is someone for whose sake his whole generation is treated favorably. Above, like רבי חנינא בן דוסא; below, like רבי אבהו in the Caesar's court.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Man of favor' is someone for whose sake his generation is shown favor. Above, in Heaven, like רבי חנינא בן דוסא. Below, on earth, like רבי אבהו at the Caesar's court.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the next term and gives two examples: one person who gets favor in Heaven, and one who gets favor from the government.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'נשוא פנים' usually means an honored person. The גמרא says it means a person whose importance brings favor to everyone in his time. That favor can come from ה׳ or from earthly rulers.

keyTerms.meaning: Man of favor, an honored person

phrases.aramaic: ״וּנְשׂוּא פָּנִים״ — זֶה שֶׁנּוֹשְׂאִין פָּנִים לְדוֹרוֹ בַּעֲבוּרוֹ.
phrases.english: 'And man of favor': this is one for whose sake favor is shown to his generation.

phrases.aramaic: לְמַעְלָה, כְּגוֹן רַבִּי חֲנִינָא בֶּן דּוֹסָא.
phrases.english: Above, such as Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa.

phrases.aramaic: לְמַטָּה, כְּגוֹן רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ בֵּי קֵיסָר.
phrases.english: Below, such as Rabbi Abbahu in the house of the Caesar.

steps.triggerLanguage: ״וּנְשׂוּא פָּנִים״ — זֶה שֶׁנּוֹשְׂאִין פָּנִים לְדוֹרוֹ בַּעֲבוּרוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the alternative reading, the גמרא moves on to the next word in the פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: נשוא פנים is someone whose merit gets favor for his generation, in Heaven or on earth.

steps.title: Counselor, wise, charmer, understanding and enchanter
steps.stepSummary: The last five terms: the counselor sets the calendar, the wise one is a student who sharpens his teachers, the charmer makes listeners like deaf people, the understanding one learns one thing from another, and the enchanter is fit to receive Torah secrets.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Counselor' is one who knows how to add leap years and set the months. 'Wise' is a student who makes his teachers wiser. 'Charmer': when he starts speaking Torah, everyone becomes like deaf people. 'Understanding' is one who figures out one thing from another. 'Enchanter' is one fit to be given the Torah that was given in a whisper.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes explaining the list in ישעיהו 3:3, giving each final word a Torah meaning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Several readings play on the sound of the word. חרשים (charmers) is linked to חרשין (deaf), because listeners can't keep up with his depth. לחש (whisper) points to the hidden parts of the תורה, which are taught quietly. Together the list shows every kind of Torah greatness that ישעיה warned would be lost.

keyTerms.meaning: To add a leap month to the year
To fix when the months begin

steps.whatToRemember: The 'supports' in ישעיה's curse are all types of Torah scholars and leaders: experts in מקרא, משנה, תלמוד and אגדה, debaters, judges, calendar experts, sharp students, and those trusted with the secrets of the תורה. The curse is losing them.

phrases.english: 'Counselor': one who knows how to make leap years and fix the months.
'And wise': this is a student who makes his teachers wise.
'Charmer': when he begins speaking words of Torah,
everyone becomes like deaf people.
phrases.notes: A play on words: חרשים sounds like חרשין, deaf. His listeners can't follow how deep he goes.

phrases.english: 'And understanding': this is one who understands one thing from another.
'Enchanter': this is one who is fit to be handed
words of Torah that were given in a whisper.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the word-by-word explanation of the list in the פסוקים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The final terms describe calendar experts, sharp students, deep teachers, careful reasoners and those trusted with Torah secrets.

steps.title: Children as princes means people empty of מצוות
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר explains 'I will make children their princes' as people who are empty of מצוות becoming the leaders.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And I will make children their princes.' What does this mean? רבי אלעזר said: these are people who are empty of מצוות.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next פסוק in ישעיהו and asks what 'children as princes' means. רבי אלעזר answers that the 'children' are people empty of מצוות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר plays on the sound of the words: נְעָרִים (children) sounds like מְנוֹעָרִין (shaken out, emptied). So the punishment is not that young people will rule. It is that spiritually empty people will rule.

keyTerms.meaning: Shaken out, emptied (here: empty of מצוות)

steps.confusionAlert: Don't read 'children' as young in age. The גמרא reads it as people empty of good deeds.

phrases.english: "And I will make children their princes."
What is meant by "And I will make children their princes"?
Rabbi Elazar said:
These are people
who are empty of מצוות.
phrases.notes: A wordplay: נערים sounds like מנוערין, 'shaken out', like a pocket with nothing left in it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the line-by-line reading of ישעיהו 3 after the list of terms in פסוקים 1-3.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'Children' who become princes are people empty of מצוות.

steps.title: Babes who rule are foxes, sons of foxes
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא בר יעקב reads תעלולים as 'foxes, sons of foxes'.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And babes shall rule over them.' רב פפא בר יעקב said: foxes, sons of foxes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the second half of the פסוק. רב פפא בר יעקב says the rulers will be 'foxes, sons of foxes'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He reads תַּעֲלוּלִים as connected to תַּעֲלָא, the Aramaic word for fox. Repeating 'sons of foxes' stresses that the low quality runs through the family too, not just the person.

keyTerms.meaning: Babes, infants (literal meaning in the פסוק)

phrases.english: "And babes shall rule over them":
Rav Pappa bar Yaakov said:
Foxes, sons of foxes.
phrases.notes: He hears תעלולים as related to תעלא, a fox.

steps.triggerLanguage: ״וְתַעֲלוּלִים יִמְשְׁלוּ בָּם״ אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא בַּר יַעֲקֹב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the second half of the same פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The 'babes' who rule are low people from low families, 'foxes, sons of foxes'.

steps.title: The empty will mock the one full of מצוות
steps.stepSummary: ישעיהו's mind was not calmed until he said that the young would be insolent to the elder. The 'young' are people empty of מצוות who mock someone full of מצוות like a pomegranate.
steps.simpleTranslation: ישעיהו was not satisfied until he said: 'The child shall be insolent to the elder, and the lowly to the honored.' People empty of מצוות will be insolent toward someone filled with מצוות like a pomegranate.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא says ישעיהו went one step further with the next פסוק. Bad people would not just rule; they would also mock the good people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'child' (נַעַר) is read the same way רבי אלעזר read נערים: someone empty of מצוות. The 'elder' is his opposite, someone packed with מצוות the way a pomegranate is packed with seeds.

keyTerms.meaning: His mind was calmed or satisfied

phrases.english: And his mind was not calmed,
until he said to them:
"The child shall act insolently against the elder,
and the lowly against the honored."

phrases.aramaic: אֵלּוּ בְּנֵי אָדָם שֶׁמְּנוֹעָרִין מִן הַמִּצְוֹת,
phrases.english: These are people who are empty of מצוות,
who will act insolently toward one who is filled
with מצוות like a pomegranate.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֹא נִתְקָרְרָה דַּעְתּוֹ עַד שֶׁאָמַר לָהֶם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes further than the last פסוק: the bad people will also mock the good.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The 'child' empty of מצוות will be insolent toward the 'elder' who is full of מצוות.

steps.title: The careless will mock the careful
steps.stepSummary: 'The lowly against the honored' means someone who treats serious sins as light will mock someone who treats even light sins as serious.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And the lowly against the honored': someone to whom serious sins seem light will come and be insolent toward someone to whom light sins seem serious.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the second half of the same פסוק. It is about two attitudes toward sin.
steps.deeperAnalysis: נִקְלֶה (lowly) is read as connected to קַלּוֹת (light things), and נִכְבָּד (honored) as connected to כָּבֵד (heavy), which is like חֲמוּרוֹת. So the 'lowly' one shrugs off big sins, while the 'honored' one is careful even about small ones.
steps.whatToRemember: In ישעיהו's picture of a broken society, the empty and careless rule over and mock the full and careful.

phrases.english: "And the lowly against the honored":
there will come one for whom serious sins
seem to him like light ones,
phrases.notes: A wordplay: נקלה sounds like קלות (light), and נכבד sounds like כבד (heavy).

phrases.english: and they will act insolently toward one for whom light sins
seem to him like serious ones.

steps.triggerLanguage: ״וְהַנִּקְלֶה בַּנִּכְבָּד״ יָבֹא מִי שֶׁחֲמוּרוֹת דּוֹמוֹת עָלָיו כְּקַלּוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes explaining ישעיהו 3:5.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Those who take serious sins lightly will mock those who take even light sins seriously.

steps.title: Trustworthy people remained even at Jerusalem's fall
steps.stepSummary: רב קטינא teaches that even at Jerusalem's downfall, trustworthy people remained. He learns this from 'You have a cloak, be our ruler,' read as 'you know the hidden Torah.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב קטינא said: even when Jerusalem was falling, trustworthy people did not disappear. The פסוק says, 'A man will grab his brother: you have a cloak, be our ruler.' This means: the things people keep covered like a cloak are in your hand.
steps.whatsHappening: רב קטינא opens a new idea from the next פסוק. Even in the worst times, honest people still existed. The גמרא starts reading the פסוק to show this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'cloak' (שִׂמְלָה) is read as Torah matters that people keep covered, like a garment covers the body. People grab someone and say, 'You know these hidden things, so lead us.' The proof of his honesty comes a few steps later, when he answers.

phrases.english: Rav Ketina said:
Even at the time of Jerusalem's downfall,
trustworthy people did not cease from among them,
as it is said:
"For a man shall take hold of his brother of his father's house:
You have a cloak, be our ruler."
Things that people keep covered like a cloak
phrases.notes: He means hidden Torah matters, kept covered the way a cloak covers you.

phrases.english: are in your hand.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב קַטִּינָא אֲפִילּוּ בִּשְׁעַת כִּשְׁלוֹנָהּ שֶׁל יְרוּשָׁלָיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to ישעיהו 3:6 with a new, more hopeful point about Jerusalem's fall.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even at Jerusalem's downfall, trustworthy people still existed.

steps.title: The stumbling block means hard Torah you master only by struggling
steps.stepSummary: 'This stumbling block' refers to Torah matters people can only understand after stumbling over them, and these too are 'in your hand'.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And this stumbling block.' What is that? Things people cannot understand unless they have stumbled over them are 'in your hand'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues with the end of the same פסוק. The people tell the man that he also knows the hardest Torah material.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מַכְשֵׁלָה (stumbling block) is read as Torah that you only grasp after you trip over it many times, meaning after hard effort. The people are praising the man as a master of both hidden and difficult Torah.

keyTerms.meaning: Understand them, get to the bottom of them

phrases.english: "And this stumbling block."
What is "and this stumbling block"?

phrases.aramaic: דְּבָרִים שֶׁאֵין בְּנֵי אָדָם עוֹמְדִין עֲלֵיהֶן
phrases.english: Things that people cannot understand
unless they have stumbled over them
"are in your hand."
phrases.notes: This is the end of the same פסוק: 'and this stumbling block is under your hand.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes reading ישעיהו 3:6 in רב קטינא's line.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The 'stumbling block' is Torah that can only be grasped through hard effort.

steps.title: He answers with an oath
steps.stepSummary: The man's answer is quoted from the next פסוק. The word ישא is shown to mean an oath, from 'לא תשא'.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'He shall swear on that day, saying: I will not be a healer, and in my house there is no bread and no cloak; do not make me ruler of the people.' ישא always means an oath, as it says: 'Do not swear falsely by the name of ה׳ your God.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the man's reply from the next פסוק. It first proves that his reply is an oath.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word יִשָּׂא is shown to mean swearing by comparing it to 'לֹא תִשָּׂא' in the עשרת הדברות, which is about oaths. So the man does not just turn down the job; he swears that he is not the scholar they think he is. That sets up the honesty point in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: A healer, one who binds wounds

phrases.english: "He shall swear on that day, saying:
I will not be a healer,
and in my house there is no bread and no cloak;
do not make me ruler of the people."
"He shall swear":
"Yissa" is nothing but a term of oath,
as it is said:
"You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the man's reply to the request from steps 30-31.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The man answers with an oath, because יִשָּׂא means swearing.

steps.title: He honestly admits he knows no Torah
steps.stepSummary: 'I will not be a חובש' means 'I never sat in the בית מדרש.' 'No bread and no cloak' means 'I have no מקרא, no משנה, and no גמרא.'
steps.simpleTranslation: 'I will not be a healer' means: I was never one of those who sit in the בית מדרש. 'In my house there is no bread and no cloak' means: I have no מקרא, no משנה, and no גמרא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what the man swore. He admits openly that he never learned and knows nothing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: חוֹבֵשׁ is read as someone who sits fixed in the בית מדרש. 'Bread' and 'cloak' stand for Torah knowledge. Instead of grabbing power by pretending to be a scholar, he swears the truth. This is רב קטינא's proof that בעלי אמנה, honest people, remained even at Jerusalem's fall.

keyTerms.meaning: Those who sit fixed in the study hall
Analysis and explanation of the משנה

steps.whatToRemember: Even when Jerusalem was spiritually at its lowest, people did not lie to gain power. When offered leadership for Torah they did not have, they swore honestly that they had no מקרא, משנה, or גמרא. That is רב קטינא's point about בעלי אמנה.
steps.confusionAlert: This is not praise for being ignorant. The praise is for being honest about it at a time when lying would have made him a ruler.

phrases.english: "I will not be a healer":
I was never one of those who sit in the study hall.
phrases.notes: חובש is being read as someone who stays put in the בית מדרש, not as a healer.

phrases.english: "And in my house there is no bread and no cloak":
for I have in hand neither Scripture
nor Mishnah nor Gemara.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains what the man swore to in step 32. This completes רב קטינא's proof.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The man truthfully swears he has no Torah knowledge, which shows honest people remained.
steps.whyThisMatters: It closes the circle on רב קטינא's claim: the honesty shown in this oath is the 'trustworthiness' that survived Jerusalem's fall.

steps.title: Maybe the man only told the truth because a lie would be exposed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the proof of רב קטינא. The man's honest answer may not show he was trustworthy, because if he had claimed to know Torah, people would have tested him on the spot.
steps.simpleTranslation: But perhaps that case is different. If he had said 'I have learned,' they would have told him, 'So teach us!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pokes a hole in the proof that trustworthy people remained. It suggests that the man admitted he knew nothing only because he had no choice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב קטינא's proof depended on the man being honest when he said he had no מקרא, משנה, or גמרא. The challenge argues that this kind of honesty proves nothing. People don't lie about things that can be checked immediately, and here they would simply have asked him to teach them.

keyTerms.meaning: Tell us! (teach us what you know)

phrases.english: But perhaps it is different there,
phrases.notes: 'There' is the story of the man who refused to be a ruler, from the earlier steps.

phrases.english: for if he had said to them, 'I have learned,'
they would say to him: 'Tell us!'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges whether the man's admission in step 33 really shows that he was trustworthy.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב קטינא's proof that trustworthy people remained in ירושלים
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Telling the truth when a lie would be exposed at once does not show that a person is trustworthy.

steps.title: He could have said he learned and forgot, so he really was honest
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the challenge. A liar could easily have said 'I learned and forgot' to avoid shame. His words 'I will not be a חובש' mean that he never learned at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: He could have said, 'I learned and forgot.' So what does 'I will not be a חובש' mean? It means, 'I will not be a healer at all,' because I never learned.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב קטינא's proof. The man had an easy way to lie without getting caught, and he still admitted the embarrassing truth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying 'I learned and forgot' could not have been tested, and it would have saved him from shame. Because he chose the full truth anyway, he really was trustworthy. The גמרא also explains that 'I will not be a חובש' does not hint that he once learned. It means he was never a 'healer' of Torah in any way.

keyTerms.meaning: Healer, one who binds wounds (here: one who sat and learned)

steps.whatToRemember: The man's honesty counts because he could have hidden behind 'I learned and forgot,' and he didn't. So רב קטינא's proof stands.

phrases.english: He could have said
'I learned and forgot.'
What is meant by 'I will not be a חובש'?
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 3:7. Literally 'I will not be one who binds wounds.' Step 33 read it as 'I never sat in the בית מדרש.'

phrases.english: I will not be a healer at all.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the challenge of step 34 and restores רב קטינא's proof.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The claim that the man's honesty was forced on him
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The man had an easy lie that could not be checked ('I learned and forgot') and still told the truth, so his honesty was real.

steps.title: רבא says ירושלים fell only after trustworthy people were gone
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא raises a contradiction. רבא says ירושלים was destroyed only after trustworthy people ceased to exist there, learning this from ירמיהו 5:1. That seems to clash with רב קטינא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that so? But רבא said: ירושלים was not destroyed until trustworthy people stopped existing in it, as it says: 'Run around the streets of ירושלים, see and know, search its squares, if you can find a man, if there is anyone who does justice and seeks truth, and I will forgive her.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets one statement against another. רב קטינא said trustworthy people remained, but רבא says none were left.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק in ירמיהו implies that not even one honest person could be found. If there had been one, ירושלים would have been forgiven. That directly contradicts רב קטינא's claim that trustworthy people remained at the time of the destruction.

phrases.english: Is that so?!
But didn't רבא say:
Jerusalem was not destroyed
until trustworthy people ceased from it,
as it is said:
'Run to and fro through the streets of Jerusalem,
and see now, and know,
and search in its open squares,
if you can find a man,
if there is anyone who acts justly,
who seeks truth, and I will forgive her'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Now that רב קטינא's proof has been defended, the גמרא challenges his conclusion from a different source.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב קטינא's statement that trustworthy people remained at the downfall of ירושלים
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבא, based on ירמיהו 5:1, says no trustworthy person was left. That directly contradicts רב קטינא.

steps.title: The גמרא says there is no contradiction
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens its answer by saying the contradiction can be resolved. The explanation itself comes on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next move. It announces that רב קטינא and רבא do not really conflict, and the explanation follows right after.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'לא קשיא' tells us both statements can be true at once. Usually this means they are talking about different situations or different kinds of trustworthiness. The details are given at the start of the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult; there is no contradiction

steps.confusionAlert: Don't stop here. The answer itself is not in this line; it continues on the next amud.

phrases.english: It is not difficult:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins the answer to רבא's contradiction from step 36.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reconciliation of two statements (details follow in the next section)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב קטינא and רבא seem to contradict each other about whether trustworthy people remained.
steps.terutzMaskana: The two statements can both be true; the explanation follows.
